extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom managers, and journalism researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate research findings about how journalists judge newsworthiness and related newsroom practices (sourcing diversity, public-opinion representation, push notifications, moderation, and social media behavior). Useful for newsroom leaders and media researchers assessing standards and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived newsworthiness by publication type
rubrics_metrics.description: Hassell found that journalists saw a story published by a national newspaper as being no more newsworthy than the same story having gone unpublished, or published by a mid-sized paper. A story published by a local newspaper was seen as less newsworthy than one that hadn’t been published at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurements showed the local-publication penalty was stronger among journalists who didn’t work for small, local papers. Possible explanations: national outlets have more resources to lead on stories others would find newsworthy, or they operate under a broader sense of newsworthiness; local outlets’ geographically narrow scope conditions other journalists to view those stories as irrelevant to their organizations. Implication: publication source (national vs local) alters journalists’ judgments in ways that may reflect perceived scope, resources, or competitive positioning rather than intrinsic story worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness perspective: audience vs editors (competitive lens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hassell measured perceived newsworthiness both in the eyes of audiences and in the eyes of editors, with the latter intended to capture competitively motivated perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of newsworthiness should consider multiple perspectives — what will interest audiences and what will be valued by editors/competitors — because each lens captures different motivations (public interest vs competitive positioning). The study found the publication-type effects held across both perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural competence and sourcing diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wenzel’s study of a U.S. public media station examined efforts to 'shift a culture of whiteness and increase the representation of people of color within both staffing and online and broadcast coverage,' including auditing and monitoring sources quoted in local stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: audit and monitor sources to reveal routinized quoting of traditional authority figures that over-represent white voices; use ethnography and sustained initiatives to change sourcing practices. Limitations/anti-patterns: single initiatives or foundation-funded efforts alone are unlikely to institutionalize change; enduring structures, white editorial leadership, and path dependencies can blunt reforms. For cultural competency to stick, practices must be routinized and supporting structures and positions strengthened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion displays: explicitness, representativeness, and citizen activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Beckers identifies three important dimensions of how public opinion appears in news: how explicitly public opinion is referenced, how representative those displays are of the larger population, and how active the role of citizens is in the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: about 1 in 5 news items referenced public opinion overall and almost half of election coverage did so; proactive real-world expressions (e.g., protests) receive little coverage; TV prefers vox pops while print favors general inferences — both approaches give journalists leeway but are not highly representative. Implication: when representing public opinion, consider method-specific biases (vox pops vs inferences) and the risk of non-representativeness; measure and disclose representativeness where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push notification temporal strategies and user-integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Wheatley and Ferrer-Conill studied more than 7,000 push notifications and focused on whether outlets try to integrate with mobile-user behavior or be disruptive to garner attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed strategies: emphasize key consumption moments (morning commutes, evening downtime) while also spreading notifications throughout the day to embed in users’ habitual 'checking cycles.' For-profit and legacy print outlets tended to use push notifications more. Practical guidance: design timing and frequency to match user behavior rather than relying solely on disruptive bursts; monitor audience rhythms and avoid overloading users. Research gap: much remains to learn about optimal rhythms and long-term effects on consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement moderation (interactive moderation rather than deletion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masullo, Riedl, and Huang define 'engagement moderation' as community managers or journalists interacting with commenters to improve comment threads, rather than deleting comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental evidence: interaction, especially using 'high-person-centered messages' that acknowledge emotional pain or frustration, reduced incivility and led readers to have more positive attitudes toward the outlet’s Facebook page, online community, and handling of incivility. Practical takeaway: prefer constructive, empathetic engagement over blanket deletion; train moderators to use person-centered responses. Anti-pattern: ignoring or only deleting comments can allow vitriol to persist or drive negative perceptions of the outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists’ social media self-disclosure: consumption vs perceived objectivity tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Lee’s experiment found that when journalists self-disclosed and interacted directly with users on social media, it increased participants’ likelihood to consume the journalist’s news updates but also reduced perceived objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Net effect in the study: the positive effect on consumption intentions outweighed the negative effect on perceived objectivity, suggesting evolving norms. Practical implication: newsrooms should weigh benefits of engagement and personal disclosure (greater audience connection and consumption) against potential erosion of perceived impartiality; update social-media guidelines to reflect changing audience expectations and to guard against partisan disclosures while allowing constructive transparency.
